results.title: hypothesis testing - Rule of Sample Proporitions - What is the minimum sample size for a 2 Proportion Z Test? - Cross Validated
results.content: # Rule of Sample Proporitions - What is the minimum sample size for a 2 Proportion Z Test? I've been reading different resources, and I've been confused over the requirements for the minimum sample sizes to perform a 2 Proportion Z-Test. Is your question about one-sample analyses or about distinguishing proportion differences between 2 samples? * $\begingroup$ @EdM - It's for distinguishing proportion differences between 2 (or more) samples. They refer to when a normal distribution is close enough to the distribution of successes in binomial sampling to allow a Z-test, which assumes a normal distribution. Binomial sampling only leads to integer numbers of successes, while the normal distribution is continuous. The 2 requirements you cite are among several rules of thumb for when a normal distribution is "close enough" to a binomial; as the Wikipedia page puts it: "the specific number varies from source to source, and depends on how good an approximation one wants.". The second issue is what sample sizes are needed to compare proportions in two or more samples. In many cases you will need more than 5 or 10 successes in each group to distinguish a difference between them. A web search for something like "two sample proportion test power calculator" will link to online tools that perform the necessary calculations. You'll note that the numbers of successes expected are well above those needed for a reasonable normal approximation to the binomial. $\begingroup$ @Shazbots that is the problem with *all* attempts to estimate the sample size needed for a study. * $\begingroup$ There are multiple rules of thumb for both one sample and two sample proportion tests (more than the ones you mention). While some can be based on meeting some specific criterion or other, typically they are not, and even when they are, that usually doesn't mean you're really getting what you're actually seeking (a close enough approximation of some p-value, power, sample size or whatever, for your purposes). results.content: # Difference in power and sample size analyses #### In This Topic * What minimum difference value do I use in a power and sample size analysis for a Z-test or t-test? * What minimum difference values do I use in a power and sample size analysis for one-way ANOVA? Difference is the smallest difference that you are interested in detecting between the hypothesized value of a population parameter and the actual value. Before you collect data for a hypothesis test or an ANOVA, you can perform a power and sample size analysis to determine whether the power is high enough to detect the difference. ## What minimum difference value do I use in a power and sample size analysis for a Z-test or t-test? In the main dialog box, you need to specify the minimum difference you are interested in detecting. For example, suppose you are testing whether or not your students' mean test score is different from the null value. * For a 2-sample t-test, express the difference as the difference between the population means that you would like to be able to detect. * For a paired t-test, express the difference as the difference between the population paired means that you would like to be able to detect. When estimating sample size, if you choose Less than as your alternative hypothesis, then you must enter a negative value in Differences. ## What minimum difference values do I use in a power and sample size analysis for one-way ANOVA? In order to calculate power or sample size, you need to estimate the difference between the smallest and largest actual factor level means. results.content: At Waziers, reducing (water logging) environment linked to the peat leads to very specific U-series data of the analysed teeth (U content lower than 0.1 ppm in all the dental tissues, evidence of leaching in some tissues), but the mean ESR/U-series age, 129 ± 4 ka, is also in agreement with the available geological and palaeoenvironmental data indicating that the dated teeth were associated with Late Glacial deposits prior to the climatic interglacial optimum. Despite a relatively poor precision by comparison to 14C or OSL results, ESR/U-series data usually enable to correlate the dated levels to a given marine isotopic stage and participate hence to the construction of a unified regional chronostratigraphical framework (Bahain et al., 2007; Antoine et al., 2000, 2007, 2014; Voinchet et al., 2015). The combined ESR/U-series analyses performed on fossil teeth collected from two Eemian sites of northern France, Caours and Waziers, demonstrate the reliability of the method to date such Middle Paleolithic sites (Fig. 5).
